title: RNNs, LSTM & GRU
html:
Recurrent networks read a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state that summarises everything seen so far. LSTMs and GRUs add gates so that memory survives over long sequences.

PatternInput → outputExample
Many-to-oneSequence → one labelSentiment of a review, activity from sensor data
One-to-manyOne input → sequenceImage captioning, music generation
Many-to-many (aligned)One output per stepPart-of-speech tagging, frame labelling
Many-to-many (seq2seq)Sequence → different-length sequenceTranslation, summarisation (encoder–decoder)

The vanilla RNN

hₜ = tanh(W_x xₜ + W_h hₜ₋₁ + b) the same weights at every time step

Training unrolls the loop and backpropagates through every step (backpropagation through time, BPTT). The gradient reaching step 1 has been multiplied by W_h and a tanh slope once per step — so over long sequences it vanishes (or explodes). A plain RNN effectively remembers only the last few steps.

LSTM and GRU

LSTMGRU
StateHidden h + separate cell c (long-term memory)Hidden h only
GatesForget, input, output (+ candidate)Update, reset (+ candidate)
Key updatec ← f ⊙ c + i ⊙ c̃ — additive, so gradients flowh ← (1 − z) ⊙ h + z ⊙ h̃
Parameters4× a vanilla RNN3× a vanilla RNN
UseThe default for long dependenciesSlightly faster, often as good

Gates are sigmoid layers (outputs between 0 and 1) that decide what to erase, what to write and what to expose. Because the cell state is updated by addition rather than repeated multiplication, information and gradients can travel across many steps — the forget gate set near 1 keeps a memory intact.

Watch out

RNNs process steps sequentially, so they can't parallelise over time and are slow on long sequences. For most language tasks Transformers replaced them; RNNs remain useful for streaming, small on-device models and some time-series work.

How does an LSTM solve the vanishing gradient problem?

Its cell state is updated additively (c = f·c + i·c̃) and controlled by gates. When the forget gate is near 1 the gradient flows back through the cell almost unchanged, instead of being squashed by a matrix and tanh at every step.

LSTM vs GRU?

GRU merges the cell and hidden state and uses two gates instead of three, so it has ~25% fewer parameters and trains faster. Performance is usually similar; LSTM can be better on very long dependencies.
